Abstract heading
States the motivating question of whether referees are biased

spans.assertion: the analysis examined the relative likelihood of darker-skinned players receiving a red card using life-history data from players in four major European leagues
using generalized linear mixed models, found that the darkest-skin-tone player was 1.38 times as likely to receive a red card as the brightest-skin-tone player
the red-card effect could stem from referee bias, a greater propensity of darker-skinned players to commit severe fouls, or a combination of both
examined country-level means of implicit and explicit racial bias as a moderator of the skin-tone effect at the level of referees' country of origin
the results for the country-level bias moderation analysis were inconclusive

spans.note: "One Sentence Summary" heading

spans.assertion: restates as the paper's one-sentence summary that darker-skinned players are more likely to get a red card

spans.note: "Results" section heading and blank line
"Data preparation" subheading

spans.assertion: the two skin-tone rater scores were averaged into a single score

the averaged skin-tone score was rescaled to a 0 (originally 1, brightest) to 1 (originally 5, darkest) range so that brightest-to-darkest differences could be read directly off regression coefficients
the new rescaled skin-tone variable was named avgrate01
cases with missing values on skin-tone rating, meanIAT, or meanExp were excluded via listwise deletion
listwise deletion was chosen so that all analyses, including research question 2, would use the same set of cases

spans.note: Restates research question 1 and interest in single-game red-card likelihood

spans.assertion: the original redCards variable was judged uninterpretable because the number of games a player has seen a given referee varies
the data were disaggregated to one row per game, with redCards coded as 1 in the first n=redCards rows per player
assumed it does not matter which specific game(s) among a player's games produced a red card, only that the correct number of red-card rows exist among that player's observations
a binomial error distribution was used because, after disaggregation, the response variable represents a 0/1 event in a single game

spans.note: Blank line and "Modeling strategy" subheading

spans.assertion: R (version 3.1.1) and the lme4 package's glmer function (version 1.1-7) were used to estimate generalized linear mixed models
the modeling approach accounts for random variance of effects across players, referees, and referees' country of origin

spans.note: Explains that the data are cross-classified rather than nested, and that lme4 can handle such structures

spans.assertion: in every model the event of getting a red card in a single game was predicted from the skin-tone variable avgrate01, while exploring different random effects and moderator variables
no covariates such as player position were used, and this approach was kept even though reviewers suggested covariates should be added

spans.note: Cites the Silberzahn et al. project description stating the data cannot be used for causal inference

spans.assertion: reasoned that for a descriptive effect-size goal it does not matter why a player accumulates more red cards, and that including such information as covariates might bias the result

spans.note: Blank line, Research Question 1 heading, blank line

spans.assertion: performed a simple visual comparison (Figure 1) of expected versus observed relative frequencies of red cards across five skin-tone categories, rounding avgrate01 values to avoid small cell frequencies
observed relative frequencies were calculated from the subset of player-game combinations in which a player received a red card (n=1589)

spans.note: Figure 1: bar chart of expected vs observed red-card frequencies by skin-tone (title, axis labels, values)

spans.assertion: observed in Figure 1 what appears to be a linear increase in red-card percentage from the lowest to the highest skin-tone category
four models were compared to test the skin-tone/red-card relationship more formally

spans.note: R code defining model gm0

spans.assertion: gm0 was specified as a reference model with only a fixed intercept plus random intercepts for refNum (referee red-card propensity) and playerShort (player red-card propensity)

spans.note: Blank line, R code defining model gm1, blank line

spans.assertion: gm1 adds a fixed effect of skin-tone (avgrate01, 0=brightest, 1=darkest)

spans.note: Blank line, R code defining model gm2, blank line

spans.assertion: gm2 adds a random effect of skin-tone across referees

spans.note: Blank line, R code defining model gm3, blank line

spans.assertion: gm3 adds a random effect of skin-tone across referees' countries of origin

spans.note: Pointer to Table 1 and blank line

spans.assertion: gm1 fit better than gm0 by AIC and a likelihood ratio test, suggesting skin-tone predicts the odds of getting a red card
gm2 was not superior to gm1 (higher AIC/BIC), suggesting the skin-tone effect does not vary across referees (near-zero variance)
gm3 fit better than gm1 by AIC and a likelihood ratio test, indicating some variance of the skin-tone effect across referees' countries of origin
chose to interpret the coefficients from gm3 as the selected model
converting the gm3 intercept to a probability gives a brightest-skin-tone player about a 0.36% chance of a red card in a single game, close to the raw mean (.0039) for that category

converting the sum of the intercept and avgrate01 coefficient to a probability gives a darkest-skin-tone player about a 0.5% chance of a red card in a single game, close to the raw mean (.0051) for that category, assuming a linear log-odds increase with skin tone
the odds of a red card were 1.38 times higher for the darkest vs brightest skin-tone category (95% Wald CI 1.10–1.75), corresponding to a small effect size (d≈0.18)

spans.note: Blank line, Research Question 2 heading, blank line

spans.assertion: visualized (scatterplot with loess line) the relationship between country-level meanIAT and gm3's random effects of avgrate01

spans.note: Figure 2: scatterplot of meanIAT vs random effects of avgrate01 from gm3

spans.assertion: Figure 2 reveals no evidence of a relationship, linear or otherwise, between country-level meanIAT and the skin-tone effect; the avgrate01×meanIAT interaction was .55 (SE=3.80, p=.89)
the meanIAT interaction odds-ratio was 1.73 with a 95% CI of 0.001 to 2983, reflecting considerable uncertainty about the true effect size

spans.note: Blank line

spans.assertion: visualized the relationship between country-level meanExp and gm3's random effects of avgrate01

spans.note: Figure 3: scatterplot of meanExp vs random effects of avgrate01 from gm3

spans.assertion: consistent with the implicit-bias result, Figure 3 shows no evidence of a relationship between meanExp and the skin-tone effect; the avgrate01×meanExp interaction was .33 (SE=.55, p=.55)
the meanExp interaction odds-ratio was 1.39
the meanExp interaction 95% CI was .47 to 4.10, indicating considerable uncertainty about the true effect size

spans.note: Blank line, Conclusion heading, blank line

spans.assertion: concluded darker skin-tone increases red-card likelihood, with darkest-category players 1.38 times as likely as brightest-category players to get a red card
the effect is stated to be consistent with several explanations: referee bias against darker-skinned players, a greater propensity of darker-skinned players to commit severe fouls, or both
an experiment showing professional referees identical fouls committed by players of different skin-tones is proposed as useful for disentangling the explanations, but was not conducted

suspected the high margin of error for the country-level bias moderation arose because most referees and players come from countries with similar racial-bias scores (especially IAT), leaving the extremes of the bias scale underrepresented
